messages.body_plain:
Hi Jerome,
Thanks for the comments - I do appreciate it.
Something else I should have mentioned, is that further down the same river where these recordings were made, a continuous recording was also being made - it ran 24hrs a day for a week. From that recording the diurnal patterns are easily seen with the ACI results, hence not understanding why there was no difference between time of day with my recordings. There are 3 main differences between the two recordings though - 1) I believe the continuous recorder had a sample rate of 44.1kHz/24bit; 2) ACI was calculated over 30 second blocks for the continuous recording rather than 1 minute; and 3) the continuous recording was continuous, whereas mine were 45min. I do not know if any of these would have any effect; the 30sec block seemed the most likely, however I will contact the designers to find out more.

Thank you for the paper recommendation. I had read it before, however was not able to view the output values - I now see my values are similar for underwater sound. I will also retry the calculation with the information you provided, I think I had used spec() rather than meanspec() in the sh() calculations.

Kind regards
Chris

messages.subject: Frequency bands as species/ species groups?
messages.subject_clean: Frequency bands as species/ species groups?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
I am new to acoustic ecology. I have been analyzing some of the large recordings (20hrs) I made during my field work in Mozambique.
I intend to get some index of species using the frequency bands.
If I understand it right, the frequency band + sound intensity / amplitude envelope in the soundscape can be considered equivalent to species in a landscape.
I need some help in understanding what is the best way of getting all the unique frequency + amplitude peaks in a large recording. Should I split the big file in to smaller segments, or is there a way to define smaller bins in a large files.

I used the mean spec function and find peaks. Is there any other way to do it?
Also, what is a good way to filter out the wind + anthrophoneic noises that I am not interested in. Will be glad for help.

regards
Hemant

A good place to get started might be the ACI function in seewave. However, you will need to study the literature on mapping acoustic complexity to species richness. It's not as simple as their being "equivalent"! Here is a paper on the subject: http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1470160X10002037

best wishes,
jesse

Hello,
So from the ACI paper, I understand that ACI is basically an indicator of community in a temporal bin. What I am looking for is a method of unsupervised spectral classification after filtering out wind + anthopophony + other non bird calls/songs. Theoretically where each peak of frequency + amplitude represents a species. It may give out of lot of false positives but then I am ready to spend time in trying to reduce that as a next step.

Can someone please guide me on this pinting out specific functions that I can use in seewave to do this. I have been playing with meanspec, spec and find peaks that sort of give me what I am looking for. but I am sure if I am doing a right thing.

Will be super grateful.

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Frequency bands as species/ species groups?
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Frequency bands as species/ species groups?
messages.body_plain:
Hemant,

If you're looking for a way to automatically quantify different species calls, a good start might be to look into the warbleR package. warbleR includes the function xcorr(), which correlates two spectrograms of interest. So you could create a template spectrogram for a given species call, then use xcorr to cross-correlate the template with segments (of length(template)) of your sample waveform. Setting a high correlation threshold (e.g. r = 0.75) would at least narrow down your data to a set of candidate sounds for further inspection. This will be computationally expensive.

There may be an analogous function in seewave but I'm not familiar with it. Hopefully that helps

Sean

messages.subject: ACI - Window Length
messages.body_plain:
Hi All

I am quite new to bioacoustics and have been playing with acoustic indices. With ACI I have been getting mixed and obscure results, and I was told that changes to the window length may help. I am curious about the best way to determine the most appropriate window length when running the script. I understand that the window length essentially changes the resolution of the spectrogram, off of which the ACI is calculated. I looked at my recordings visually and played around with the spectral displays to find a window length that appeared to show individual bird calls most clearly without blurring them out or chopping them up. I then used that as the window length in R for ACI. Does this sound like a reasonable approach and does anyone have advice on determining the best window length to use? Has anyone else noticed significant changes in the outcomes with changes to window length?

Thank you!

Laura

messages.subject: Re: ACI - Window Length
messages.body_plain:
Laura,

With regard to choosing the best window settings, I've been told to use the window length/overlap that allows you to best pick out the information you're interested in, and then stay consistent with them. The Pieretti et al. 2008 <http://s3.amazonaws.com/academia.edu.documents/43017888/A_new_methodology_to_infer_the_singing_a20160224-15736-12qv9r0.pdf?AWSAccessKeyId=AKIAIWOWYYGZ2Y53UL3A&Expires=1490854560&Signature=7rXjKfqGLrFiPJ%2Bmb%2Fu%2Fh%2FP40Uk%3D&response-content-disposition=inline%3B%20filename%3DA_new_methodology_to_infer_the_singing_a.pdf> paper uses a window length of 512 points, so it might be best to stick with the default setting for the ACI function.

Here's a resource <https://www.spectraplus.com/DT_help/overlap_percentage.htm> that helped me conceptualize the process. I'm not an expert, so it might require some digging in the literature to see what other people have already done.

Sean
